summary: Provides an experimental update to TCP for traffic where the sending rate is limited by the application and not by congestion. It lets a sender restart quickly after such a quiet period while still reacting properly to congestion.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP's congestion window decides how much data a sender may have in flight. When an application has nothing to send, the window should not keep growing, but standard TCP lets it. This document keeps a recently used window for a while and then trims it back if it turns out to be too large.

subtitle: How a TCP sender that is not using its full congestion window can keep a recent window safely, without growing a stale one.

tldr.problem: When an application sends more slowly than its congestion window allows, standard TCP lets the window grow far beyond what the path was really carrying, which wastes capacity and can cause congestion.
tldr.mechanism: The method measures how much data the network acknowledged in one round-trip time and compares it with half the window, keeping a recently used window while the sender is rate-limited but resetting it if congestion appears.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document that obsoletes RFC 2861 and reclassifies that document from Experimental to Historic, because the earlier method was too conservative for applications that vary their sending rate.

facts.label: Window at end of loss recovery

today: RFC 7661 is an Experimental document and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 2861, whose status it changes from Experimental to Historic, because the earlier congestion window validation method was found to be too conservative for applications that vary their sending rate.

sections.title: Why Rate-Limited Traffic Upsets TCP
sections.content:
TCP is used for traffic with a wide range of application behaviours. The congestion window, cwnd, controls the maximum number of unacknowledged packets or bytes a flow may have in the network at any time, a value known as the FlightSize. A bulk application always has data ready, so the rate at which it sends is limited by the receiver's advertised window and by cwnd, and the FlightSize of a bulk flow grows with the cwnd and tracks the volume of data acknowledged in the last round-trip time.

A rate-limited application is different. It has periods when the sender is idle, or able to send only at a rate below what cwnd allows. The volume of data in flight can then change significantly from one round-trip time to the next and can be much less than cwnd, so the FlightSize can significantly exceed the recently used capacity.

Standard TCP tells a sender to set cwnd to no more than the Restart Window before it begins transmitting if it has not sent data for longer than the retransmission timeout. The document notes that this behaviour was not always observed in implementations, and that experiments confirm it is still the case. Congestion Window Validation in RFC 2861 introduced the term application-limited period for the time when the sender sends less than the congestion or receiver windows allow, and described a method to support applications that vary their transmission rate. Many Internet applications behave this way, including web browsing, HTTP-based adaptive streaming, query and response protocols, network file sharing, and live video transmission, and many of them avoid long-lived persistent connections for exactly this reason, using a succession of short transfers or UDP instead.

Standard TCP imposes no additional restriction on the growth of cwnd when a sender cannot send at the maximum rate the window allows, so a rate-limited sender may grow a cwnd far beyond the current transmit rate. Such an invalid cwnd can reduce application performance and can significantly contribute to network congestion. The goals of the update are not to change the behaviour of a bulk sender that fully uses its window, to coexist with standard TCP and with other flows using the updated method, to reduce transfer latency for applications that change rate over short intervals, to avoid growing a large non-validated cwnd that has not recently been used, to remove the incentive for padding a stream just to keep a large window, and to give applications a reason to use long-lived connections rather than a succession of short-lived flows.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP keeps a note of how much data may be in flight at once. If an application has nothing to send, that note can keep growing even though the network never carried that much. The document wants to keep the note useful without letting it run away.

sections.title: Why the Earlier Method Was Retired
sections.content:
RFC 2861 described a simple modification to the TCP congestion control algorithm that decayed the cwnd after a transition to a sufficiently long idle period, using the slow-start threshold to save information about the previous value of the congestion window. This relaxed the standard TCP behaviour for an idle session, and also modified behaviour when a sender transmitted at a rate below what cwnd allowed.

The earlier document proposed two sets of responses, one after an application-limited period and one after an idle period. In practice, telling the two conditions apart was found to be problematic in real networks. The approach gave predictable performance for long on-off periods, much longer than one round-trip time, or for slowly varying rate-based traffic, but performance could be unpredictable for variable-rate traffic, and it depended both on whether an accurate round-trip time had been obtained and on the pattern of the application traffic relative to the measured round-trip time.

Many applications can and often do vary their transmission over a wide range of rates, and with the earlier method such applications often experienced varying performance, which made it hard for application developers to predict TCP latency even on a path with stable network characteristics. The document argues that classifying application behaviour as application-limited or idle is problematic and inappropriate, and so it treats all rate-limited traffic uniformly.

The method was implemented as the default behaviour in some mainstream operating systems, and analysis has shown that a sender using it can use available capacity on a shared path after an idle period, which can benefit variable-rate applications over long delay paths compared with the slow-start restart of standard TCP. But it would only benefit an application if the idle period were shorter than several retransmission timeout intervals, since beyond that the behaviour matches standard TCP, which resets cwnd to the TCP Restart Window.

Some operating systems supported non-standard methods instead, and applications resorted to padding streams, sending dummy data to keep their sending rate up. Padding does give good evidence that the path can sustain the offered rate, but it consumes network capacity and reduces the opportunity for congestion-free statistical multiplexing, which matters for variable-rate flows. The conclusion reached was that the earlier method had the correct motivation but the wrong approach: it benefited the network by reducing the probability of congestion, but its behaviour was too conservative for common rate-limited applications and it was unclear whether applications actually used it on the general Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier method tried to tell apart two cases, an application that pauses and one that sends slowly. In real networks that distinction proved unreliable, so the behaviour became unpredictable for the applications that vary their rate most. This document stops drawing the distinction.

sections.title: The Terms the Method Introduces
sections.content:
The document assumes familiarity with the terminology of TCP congestion control and adds a handful of terms. A flow is cwnd-limited when it has sent the maximum number of segments permitted by cwnd and the application uses the allowed sending rate. A pipeACK sample is a measure of the volume of data acknowledged by the network within a round-trip time. The pipeACK variable measures the available capacity using the set of pipeACK samples. The pipeACK Sampling Period is the maximum period that a measured pipeACK sample may influence the pipeACK variable.

A rate-limited flow is one that does not consume more than one half of cwnd and hence operates in the non-validated phase; this includes periods when the application is idle and periods when it chooses to send at less than the maximum rate permitted by cwnd. The non-validated phase is the phase in which cwnd reflects a previous measurement of the available path capacity. The non-validated period is the maximum period for which cwnd is preserved in that phase. The validated phase is the phase in which cwnd reflects a current estimate of the available path capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: The new words describe two things: how much the network actually acknowledged in the last round trip, and whether the window still matches that. A window that has not been checked recently is called non-validated.

sections.title: The New Congestion Window Validation Method
sections.content:
The method is a sender-side-only change to TCP congestion control. It creates a new protocol state, and the sender must determine when the window is validated or non-validated to control entry and exit from that state. It does not differentiate between a sender that has become idle and one that is sending below the rate cwnd allows.

A sender starts a connection in the validated phase and initialises the pipeACK variable to the undefined value, which inhibits its use in cwnd calculations. To estimate the validated capacity of a path, the sender introduces pipeACK, which differs from FlightSize in that it is evaluated over a window of acknowledged data rather than reflecting the amount of data outstanding. A pipeACK sample is measured by the volume of data acknowledged by the network over the period of a measured round-trip time. The sender should take at least one sample per round-trip time when it has unacknowledged segments. The pipeACK variable may consider multiple samples over the pipeACK Sampling Period but must not exceed the highest value within that period, which the document defines as Max(3*RTT, 1 second). When no measurements are available, the variable is set to the undefined value, which inhibits entering the non-validated phase. The variable must not be updated during TCP Fast Recovery, and the document recommends the SACK option and the recovery method of RFC 6675.

The two phases are defined by a comparison. The sender is in the validated phase when pipeACK is at least half of cwnd, or when pipeACK is undefined, which is the normal phase in which the standard methods increase cwnd. It is in the non-validated phase when pipeACK is less than half of cwnd, meaning the window is based on a previous measurement whose use has not been validated within the pipeACK Sampling Period. The threshold of one half was chosen because a sender in slow-start is permitted to double its FlightSize from one round-trip time to the next, so a sender whose FlightSize is below half of cwnd must be treated as non-validated and needs additional mechanisms.

On entering the non-validated phase the sender preserves cwnd: it only increases after fully using the window in this phase, and otherwise the window neither grows nor reduces. The phase ends when the sender transmits enough data that pipeACK exceeds half of cwnd, or when it sees an indication of congestion. After a fixed period, the non-validated period, the sender adjusts cwnd. That period should not exceed five minutes. While in the phase, a sender that is cwnd-limited may use the standard method to increase cwnd, but one that is not cwnd-limited must not increase it on receipt of ACKs, so it avoids growing a window it has not recently used. If congestion is detected the sender must exit the phase, reducing cwnd as specified. If the retransmission timeout expires the sender must also exit the phase and resume the standard TCP RTO mechanism. A sender with pipeACK above half of cwnd should enter the validated phase, which releases it from the constraints on cwnd growth.

Response to congestion. Receiving congestion feedback in the non-validated phase is read as a sign that it was wrong to use the preserved window, so the sender must reduce the rate quickly. Because the window has no validated value, a new one is selected from the utilised rate. On detecting a packet drop the sender records the current FlightSize in LossFlightSize and calculates a safe window for loss recovery as cwnd = (Max(pipeACK,LossFlightSize))/2. At the end of the recovery phase the sender must reset the window with cwnd = (Max(pipeACK,LossFlightSize) - R)/2, where R is the volume of data successfully retransmitted during recovery. The result must not be reduced below one TCP Maximum Segment Size. After loss recovery the sender must re-initialise pipeACK to the undefined value, so standard TCP methods apply until a new sample can be taken, and ssthresh is adjusted by the standard method.

Burst control. Congestion control lets a sender accumulate a window that allows a burst of segments up to the difference between the FlightSize and cwnd, and such bursts can hurt other flows sharing a bottleneck or cause congestion where buffering is limited. The document recommends that a sender in the non-validated phase control the maximum burst size, for example by pacing the window out over its estimate of the round-trip time, without recommending any specific method.

End of the period. If the application stays in the non-validated phase for longer than the non-validated period, and the sender then exits the phase, it must update ssthresh to max(ssthresh, 3*cwnd/4), recording that the present rate was safely sustained, and then update cwnd to not greater than max((1/2)*cwnd, IW), where IW is the appropriate TCP initial window. These adjustments put the sender into slow-start, and halve the window relative to the preserved value.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender watches how much the network acknowledges over one round trip and compares that with half its window. If the two roughly match, the window is trusted. If the acknowledged amount is much smaller, the window is kept but not allowed to grow, and it is trimmed back when the sender next sends. Any sign of congestion brings the window down at once.

sections.title: Choosing a Safe Period to Keep the Window
sections.content:
Limiting the period during which cwnd may be preserved avoids the side effects that come with keeping it unnecessarily high for an arbitrary period, which was part of the problem the earlier method tried to address. The period a sender may safely preserve cwnd is a function of how long a network path is expected to sustain the capacity the window reflects, and there is no ideal choice.

Five minutes was chosen. It is a compromise that is longer than the idle intervals of common applications but not much longer than the period for which the capacity of an Internet path may commonly be regarded as stable. The capacity of wired networks is usually relatively stable over several minutes, and that stability increases with capacity, which suggests cwnd may be preserved for at least a few minutes.

There are cases where TCP throughput varies significantly over less than five minutes. Wireless topologies are an example, where rate variations may fluctuate on the order of a few seconds as a consequence of medium access protocol instabilities, and mobility changes may also affect TCP performance over short time scales. Senders that observe such rapid changes may experience increased congestion with the new method, although such variation would likely also affect TCP behaviour when supporting interactive and bulk applications. Routing algorithms may change the path a transport uses, which can disrupt the round-trip time measurement and change the capacity available, but the document assumes such path changes do not usually occur frequently compared with a time frame of a few minutes.

Simulation studies suggest that for many practical applications the performance using this value will not be significantly different from that observed with a non-standard method that does not reset cwnd after an idle period. Other TCP sender mechanisms have used a five-minute timer, so reusing the same interval could simplify some implementations, and TCP defines a default user timeout of five minutes, which is how long transmitted data may remain unacknowledged before a connection is forcefully closed.
sections.plainLanguage: The window is kept for at most five minutes. That is long enough for most applications to be briefly busy, and short enough that a path whose capacity has changed is not trusted for long.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The general security considerations concerning TCP congestion control are discussed in RFC 5681. This document describes an algorithm that updates one aspect of the congestion control procedures, so the considerations described in that document apply to this algorithm as well. The document adds nothing beyond that.
sections.plainLanguage: The document says only that the usual TCP congestion control security considerations apply, because the change touches one part of the congestion control procedures.
